The Mediterranean short-toed lark (Alaudala rufescens) is a small passerine that inhabits arid and semi-arid lowlands across southern Europe, North Africa, and parts of the Middle East. Field studies conducted in coastal dune systems have provided detailed data on its early development, particularly under controlled incubation conditions. Eggs maintained at an incubation temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] required a developmental period of 13 days [ab = 13 days] before hatching, a duration that falls within the typical range of 12 to 14 days reported for the species. The newly hatched nestlings emerge with an initial wet body mass of just 4.09 grams [Ww0 = 4.09 grams], a value consistent with the altricial pattern of development observed across the Alaudidae family. This modest mass at hatching necessitates intense parental provisioning throughout the subsequent nestling stage, a period during which chicks remain entirely dependent on their parents for thermoregulation and food delivery. The energetic demands placed on the adults during this critical phase are substantial, as they must sustain both their own metabolism and the rapid growth of their offspring.

Adult females eventually reach an asymptotic mass of 24.1 grams [Wwi = 24.1 grams], representing the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown breeding individuals. This body size places the Mediterranean short-toed lark near the middle of the size range for the genus Alaudala, being notably larger than the congeneric Alaudala cheleensis but smaller than Alaudala somalica. The species exhibits a relatively slow life-history pace compared to other small passerines of comparable mass, a trait that is reflected in its extended maximum longevity. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period in this species, which centers around a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated at approximately 4124 days [am = approximately 4124 days]. This considerable longevity, unusual for a bird of its size, likely reflects the relatively low extrinsic mortality rates typical of stable arid environments where predation pressure may be reduced compared to more mesic habitats.

Energetic investigations using flow-through respirometry have characterized the basal metabolic rate of the Mediterranean short-toed lark. Measurements taken from adult individuals held within their thermoneutral zone at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] revealed a resting oxygen consumption rate of 66.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 66.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, when standardized against the species mean adult body mass, yields a metabolic rate that is somewhat elevated compared to predictions from standard allometric equations for passerines of similar size, a pattern often observed in birds inhabiting open, exposed environments where thermoregulatory costs may be higher. The measurement reflects the energetic costs associated with maintaining basal physiological functions and serves as a critical reference point for understanding the species overall energy budget. During the breeding season, these metabolic demands must be met alongside the considerable energy expenditure required for territorial defense, mate attraction, and the provisioning of dependent young in the nest.

Reproductive output in the Mediterranean short-toed lark is characterized by a conservative strategy. Clutches typically consist of two to five eggs per nest [N_R_i = two to five eggs per nest], and females usually raise a single brood each year [F_R_i = a single brood each year]. This low annual reproductive rate, combined with the substantial investment in parental care, aligns with the species relatively long lifespan. The timing of the first breeding event is a critical life-history milestone. In populations inhabiting the Iberian Peninsula, field observations indicate that the first successful nesting attempt occurs approximately 365 days after the individual's own hatching date [tR = approximately 365 days after the individual's own hatching date], a timing that synchronizes reproduction with the following at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] spring season. The onset of sexual maturity precedes this first breeding event by a considerable interval, with young birds reaching puberty at around 45 days after hatching [tp = around 45 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This pronounced gap between physiological maturation and actual reproductive activity is a common pattern in long-lived species that require extensive learning or territory establishment before they can successfully breed.

The developmental trajectory of the nestling period culminates in fledging, an event that marks the transition from nest dependence to a brief period of post-fledging care. Under the thermoneutral conditions characteristic of the adult active metabolic state, defined by a core body temperature near 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], young birds typically achieve their first sustained flight and depart the nest at 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching]. This fledging period is relatively brief for a passerine of this body size and likely reflects an adaptive response to high nest predation risk in open habitats. After fledging, the young remain dependent on their parents for food for an additional several weeks, during which time they refine their foraging skills and gradually achieve nutritional independence. The rapid early growth, modest adult size, and extended lifespan of the Mediterranean short-toed lark collectively illustrate a life-history strategy that balances high early mortality risk against the potential for many years of reproductive effort in a challenging environment.
